title: Improving detection of invasive ants using below‐ground monitoring tools
content:
We found below-ground lures to be more effective at detecting Darwin's ant (Doleromyrma darwiniana), a pest ant species, than lures deployed above-ground. We demonstrate that by taking foraging behaviour into account, detection at low density can be improved, thereby enhancing the probability of ant eradication. The new below-ground deployment lure we have developed for pest ant management could be applied globally to pest ant management programmes, particularly where poor detection at low density is hindering eradication.


Abstract

Invasive ants can cause enormous damage across multiple sectors and are targeted by eradication programmes where infestations are relatively small, to prevent spread and impact. However, ant eradication programmes can fail if detection and control techniques do not target species-specific behaviours. Existing techniques for detecting invasive ants at low density (new incursions or the ‘mop-up’ final phase of eradication) assume ants are foraging above-ground. While tools and devices deployed above-ground are effective for many species, some ant species forage below-ground and can be difficult to detect above-ground at low density using these methods. Darwin's ant (Doleromyrma darwiniana), a pest ant species in New Zealand, offers a unique opportunity to investigate the deployment of below-ground lures for improved species-specific management. This species appears to forage below-ground more than other pest ant species currently managed in New Zealand, making eradication difficult. Here, we tested whether below-ground lures are more effective at detecting Darwin's ant than lures deployed above-ground. First, we used several lure types that are commonly used as ant attractants (carbohydrate, lipid, protein, combination) and presented these above- and below-ground to compare relative effectiveness in attracting Darwin's ants. Second, we took the most attractive treatment (comprising lure type and presentation method) and tested this against the current best industry practice for monitoring (a commercial non-toxic protein lure presented above-ground) in low-density detection trials. We found the odds of detection with our newly tested treatment (carbohydrate, below-ground) were 2.5 times better than the above-ground current best industry practice. Practical implication. We demonstrate that by taking foraging behaviour into account, detection at low density can be improved, thereby enhancing the probability of ant eradication. The new below-ground deployment lure we have developed for pest ant management could be applied globally to pest ant management programmes, particularly where poor detection at low density is hindering eradication.
